clinicalPearls: A mucin-producing cystic neoplasm arising from the pancreatic ductal epithelium, with malignant potential
It is classified as main-duct, branch-duct or mixed type, which differ substantially in cancer risk
Many are found incidentally on cross-sectional imaging as pancreatic cysts communicating with the duct
Main-duct and mixed types carry a high risk of malignancy and generally warrant resection
Worrisome and high-risk features (such as a dilated main duct, an enhancing mural nodule or obstructive jaundice) guide management
Branch-duct lesions without high-risk features are often kept under surveillance
reference.pathophysiology: Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms are proliferations of mucin-secreting epithelium within the pancreatic ducts, producing papillary growth and cystic ductal dilatation from mucin accumulation. They represent a spectrum from low-grade dysplasia to invasive carcinoma, following an adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence. Main-duct involvement reflects more extensive, higher-grade disease with greater malignant potential, whereas branch-duct lesions are generally lower risk. Mucin extrusion from a patulous papilla may be seen endoscopically.
additionalDifferentials: Mucinous cystic neoplasm of the pancreas
additionalInvestigations: Cross-sectional imaging (CT/MRI with MRCP) characterising duct communication and features
Endoscopic ultrasound with cyst fluid analysis where indicated
Assessment of worrisome and high-risk stigmata
Surveillance imaging for low-risk branch-duct lesions
redFlags: Obstructive jaundice from a lesion in the pancreatic head
An enhancing mural nodule or markedly dilated main duct
Rapid cyst growth or new solid component
New-onset or worsening diabetes or weight loss
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent for resected non-invasive lesions, but invasive IPMN carries a prognosis related to the associated carcinoma; appropriate surveillance and timely resection are key.
pitfalls: Misclassifying a mucinous cystic neoplasm or pseudocyst as IPMN
Under-recognising the high malignant risk of main-duct disease
Discontinuing surveillance of branch-duct lesions prematurely
Overlooking worrisome features that should prompt resection
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Resect main-duct and mixed-type lesions, for example by pancreatoduodenectomy or distal pancreatectomy, given their high malignant potential
Resect branch-duct lesions harbouring worrisome or high-risk features such as an enhancing mural nodule, dilated main duct or obstructive jaundice
Keep low-risk branch-duct lesions under structured surveillance imaging with MRI and MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound
Use endoscopic ultrasound with cyst-fluid analysis to clarify indeterminate lesions
Individualise resection versus surveillance decisions through multidisciplinary review
Continue surveillance of the pancreatic remnant for metachronous disease and manage pancreatic exocrine insufficiency with enzyme replacement after resection
